executive_summary:
AUD/CHF closed at 0.57979 on 30 October 2026, quoted as Swiss francs per Australian dollar, so a rising rate means a stronger Australian dollar. The pair is up 0.65% over one month, 1.71% over three months, 3.06% over six months and 11.06% over a year. It sits at the 91st percentile of its 52-week closing range, 14 pips below the lower edge of the seven-touch resistance band at 0.58123-0.58585 that capped the September high.

The pair rests on two things at once. It has the widest policy differential in the G10: 460bp now, and 485bp if the RBA hikes on 3 November as expected. It is also funded in a currency whose safe-haven role came back hard in October, when the French bond rout led several dealers to question the franc as a funding leg. Neither standalone view shows the bilateral feature that matters most: AUD/CHF has double beta to risk. Risk-off sells the Australian dollar and buys the franc at the same time. Options on both dollar legs price that tail in the same direction.

On that basis the tactical stance is Neutral, conviction 2, with a weighted score of +0.084. Carry, positioning and a hawkish RBA almost exactly offset deteriorating credit, a soft China and the franc's haven bid. The strategic stance is Bearish, conviction 2, at -0.1411. Five slower factors outweigh the carry advantage over one to six months: Australia's record external deficit against Switzerland's 9% of GDP surplus, a 2027 SNB hike option, Australian growth weakness, event risk and dollar funding.

The main caveat is cost. The pair's futures roll discounts about 5.1% a year, which puts the six-month forward near 0.5651, inside the six-touch support band at 0.56309-0.5672. The bearish drift we expect is therefore mostly priced already. On our probability-weighted path an outright short loses money after carry. The view is better expressed by cutting carry longs into strength at 0.5812-0.5859 than by selling the cross outright.

One more warning for timing. Twenty-day realised volatility of 8.74% is running above the estimated one-month implied volatility of 7.293%. Four of the five largest daily moves in the last six months were declines. The 3 November cluster (RBA decision, Swiss CPI and the US midterms) arrives with that left tail already showing in the chart.

market_context.valuation_assessment: Real exchange rates and PPP point in opposite directions for this cross. On recent history the Australian dollar is real-expensive and the franc real-cheap, which supports the strategic external-balance case. World Bank 2025 PPP fair value is about 0.6653, so spot is 12.9% below PPP (PPP is 14.8% above spot); PPP gaps of this size have no record of closing on a one-to-six-month horizon and are not weighted. The 52-week range on a closing basis is 0.51634-0.58634 (high 17 September); on an intraday basis 0.51292-0.58827 (high 18 September), where spot is at the 89th percentile.

market_context.recent_regime: The cross has been a carry vehicle interrupted by haven shocks. On 1 October it fell from 0.58248 to 0.57337 intraday during the French bond rout, showing that anyone funding carry in francs carries a risk that can move five standard deviations in a day; hedge funds caught in the French bond slump were forced to unwind bets rapidly. A second drop on 15 October coincided with iron ore's two-year low. Each time the pair recovered within days on RBA repricing, reaching 0.58456 on 28 October after the hot Australian CPI. As late as 30 October the franc was still described as under pressure from carry trades exploiting wide rate gaps. The dominant narrative is a contest between the widest carry in the G10 and a funding currency that has regained haven credibility.

bilateral_carry_analysis.carry_assessment: The policy differential is 460bp (RBA 4.60%, SNB 0.00%), widening to 485bp if the RBA hikes on 3 November; the 2-year spread is about 475bp. The CME futures calendar roll (Dec 2026 to Mar 2027 contracts, observed 29 October) is 508.7bp annualised in favour of a long, which includes the expected November hike and any cross-currency basis (not separable without an OIS curve). Carry-to-volatility is 0.66 on the 508.7bp roll over the 7.653% three-month implied estimate; on the 460bp policy differential it is 0.60, on 20-day realised vol (8.74%) 0.53 and on 60-day realised (7.06%) 0.65. Because the implied estimate runs low, the true implied-basis ratio is probably 0.52-0.55, still the best in the G10 on a policy-rate basis. Carry is working: the pair rose 11.06% over the year on top of about 4.6% of carry, but the regime pays steadily and gives back abruptly: the 15 October fall of 98 pips erased more than four months of carry in one session. One month of carry is roughly half an ATR(14) of 47 pips.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: AUD/CHF has the widest policy gap in the G10. The RBA Cash Rate Target is 4.60% and the SNB policy rate is 0%, a 460bp gap. The 2-year spread is about 475bp (Australia 4.93%, Switzerland 0.18% on 30 October) and the 10-year about 467bp (5.137% against 0.47%). Inside four weeks only the Australian side can move it. The RBA decides on 3 November, all four major Australian banks now expect a 25bp hike to 4.85%, and money markets on 1 November priced about 79-81% of that move, roughly 20bp of the 25bp. The SNB does not meet until 10 December, outside the tactical window, and only about 6bp of tightening was priced for that meeting in mid-October. So delivery itself leaves only about 5bp unpriced. The larger edge is in guidance: twelve-month pricing of only about 0.9 hikes in total means the market already treats November as roughly the last move, so a Board that keeps an explicit tightening bias in its new forecasts would add to the expected gap, not just confirm it. The transmission is carry. A 460-485bp gap against an estimated three-month implied volatility of 7.653% gives a carry-to-volatility ratio near 0.60, the best in the G10, which keeps AUD/CHF the preferred long in franc-funded carry while volatility stays low. The risk to the stance is a hold on 3 November, about one chance in five on market pricing, which would take roughly 20bp off the Australian front end at once.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months the level of the gap matters more than its next step. After a November hike the gap would be 485bp. The scheduled decisions in the window are the RBA on 8 December and 9 February and the SNB's quarterly assessment on 10 December, and none of them is expected to change it in the central case. The AUD dossier puts the RBA peak at 4.85%, with a 35% chance of 5.10% by March 2027. The CHF dossier gives a 30% chance of a first SNB hike in March 2027, at a meeting after the last date on the published schedule used here, so it cannot be tied to a fixed date. Those two tails roughly offset, leaving a stable 485bp central path. The 10 December SNB forecast round is the first scheduled point at which the Swiss side could narrow it. Importantly, the market already prices the Australian peak. With only about 0.9 hikes priced over twelve months there is little second hike left to unwind, which removes much of the strategic downside the AUD dossier identified in its rate path. The rolled CME futures discount between the December and March contracts is about 508.7bp annualised. That is above the policy gap because it includes the expected November hike and any cross-currency basis, and it shows a long earns roughly 5% a year to hold. Carry stays strongly positive for the pair. But a gap that has stopped widening loses its expectations-channel support, so confidence is lower than tactically.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The inflation gap is very wide. Australian monthly CPI was 4.3% in September and the September-quarter trimmed mean 3.7%, against Swiss headline CPI of 1.0% and core of 0.5%. That gap is the reason the RBA is hiking and the SNB is not. Growth momentum is moving the other way. Australian employment fell 39,300 in September, unemployment rose for a third month to 4.7%, and the October composite PMI dropped to 47.7. Switzerland's indicators are easing from a high level: the KOF barometer is at 107.6, the procure.ch PMI at 55.3 and unemployment at 3.1%. Inside four weeks the hot Australian inflation is absorbed by the 3 November hike, and the labour data limit what follows, so the two cancel out. The asymmetry is that Australian data move this pair more, because the RBA path is live while the SNB is anchored at zero. The October labour force in the third week of November and the 25 November monthly CPI decide which side wins. The 3 November Swiss CPI matters only at the extremes: a print of 1.2% or more would revive SNB hike pricing and weigh on the pair, and 0.8% or less would support it.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months the two economies are in different phases, and the policy implications converge. Australia shows late-cycle stagflation. Inflation is cost-push (fuel, electricity, goods at 4.6%), services are not accelerating, real wages are falling and unemployment has risen three months running. That mix usually ends with a central bank stopping early, and Deputy Governor Hauser has already said past hikes are weighing on activity. Switzerland is moving the other way from the lowest inflation base in the G10. Headline CPI rose to 1.0%, the SNB's own forecast has inflation higher in the fourth quarter, and oil above USD 110 puts early-2027 risk at 1.2-1.5%, which opens a 2027 hike option the Swiss curve barely prices. So each economy's data push its central bank toward the other's position: Australian growth weakness argues for a peak, Swiss inflation for a lift-off. That narrows the expected differential at the margin and weighs on the pair. The 2 December Australian September-quarter GDP, expected by the AUD dossier at 0.2-0.3% q/q, is the main dated test. Confidence is capped at 55 because Swiss growth is distorted by pharmaceutical swings and Australian inflation expectations at 5.3% could still force more hikes.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: In this pair, risk appetite pushes both legs the same way. Risk-off weakens the Australian dollar through its equity and China beta and strengthens the franc as a haven, so the cross moves roughly twice as much as either leg does against the dollar. Risk appetite is worse than the equity index levels suggest. US high-yield spreads are 326bp and investment-grade 89bp, at the 95th and 96th percentiles of their one-year ranges. Semiconductors fell 6.7% on 22 October on doubts over AI spending. China's October manufacturing PMI slipped to 49.3. European sovereign stress has brought back the franc's haven role, with the OAT-Bund spread at 152.5bp after a high near 159bp. Against that, the VIX at 17.2 is only middling, the SMI rose 8.7% in October and gold fell 7%, which takes away one of the franc's usual supports. The US midterms on 3 November add a binary on the same day as the RBA decision. Weakening credit, a soft China and an active haven bid for the franc make the four-week skew negative for the pair, and both dossiers lean the same way: the AUD dossier is Bearish AUD on risk and the CHF dossier Bullish CHF.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over six months the risk regime is genuinely two-sided for this cross. The bear case is that wide credit spreads, doubts over AI capital spending and an oil shock with Brent above USD 110 turn into a global slowdown, in which this pair usually falls hardest of the major crosses. The bull case is that the S&P 500 is still up about 11% this year, China's third-quarter GDP beat at 4.5%, and a Hormuz settlement would be a strong positive supply shock that lifts the Australian dollar and drains haven demand for the franc at the same time. Gold falling from its highs and the SNB's own note that haven demand was limited in the third quarter suggest the franc's haven premium is not structurally rising. The French spread stress mainly drives EUR/CHF and reaches AUD/CHF only weakly. Both dossiers score this factor Neutral strategically, and their scenario weights put the risk-off and risk-on tails at about 25% each. With the tails balanced there is no directional signal. A move in US high-yield spreads above 400bp would turn it Bearish, and a fall below 280bp Bullish.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: Speculators are short both legs, but not equally. In the week to 27 October, asset managers were net short 125,237 Australian-dollar contracts, about USD 8.8bn, and the legacy non-commercial net short of 128,300 contracts is beyond the -80,000 level that has historically marked Australian-dollar extremes. In the franc, leveraged funds were net short 17,502 contracts, the most in 25 weeks, but well short of the roughly 30,000-contract scale that has preceded franc squeezes. Asset managers' franc short of 25,067 is the smallest in that window. The more extreme leg is therefore the Australian dollar short, and it faces a dated catalyst: a hawkish 3 November decision, with about 20% of the hike still unpriced and the guidance open, is the classic trigger for covering. The offset is that leveraged funds are long the Australian dollar by 48,414 contracts and short the franc, so fast money is effectively long this pair as a carry trade, and a risk-off unwind would hit it. Options agree on the direction of hedging: Australian-dollar puts and franc calls are both bid in one-month 25-delta risk reversals, so protection against the pair falling is already well owned. On balance the short base and its catalyst make the near-term response asymmetric to the upside.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over six months positioning cuts both ways for the pair. The Australian dollar short is extreme, but it was built on a real terms-of-trade loss: iron ore near a two-year low and a record current-account deficit. In the AUD dossier's 2015 and 2019 analogues, shorts of this kind were held for two to three quarters before covering. So it is more a floor under the downside than a source of upside. On the franc side, asset managers have already covered 42% of their July short, and the CHF dossier warns they could rebuild hedges toward -43,000 contracts if European stress fades, which would support the pair. If stress instead deepens, the leveraged-fund franc short, built steadily alongside the widening carry gap, would cover and weigh on the pair. The pair's fast-money carry long is the most vulnerable position in an abrupt risk shock. Japanese and other real-money demand for Australian bonds and Swiss institutional hedging of foreign assets are slow-moving structural flows that roughly offset. With extremes on one leg counterbalanced by unwind risk in the carry trade itself, there is no clear six-month signal.

tactical.unwind_trigger: A hawkish 3 November RBA decision that keeps an explicit tightening bias would trigger Australian-dollar short covering and lift the pair. tactical.contrarian_case: The crowd is short the Australian dollar on terms of trade and right on fundamentals, but the positioning is late. With about one-fifth of the hike unpriced and twelve-month pricing already treating November as the last move, any hint from the RBA of further tightening forces covering into a market where downside hedges are already bid. The contrarian trade is that the next surprise for this pair is upward, not downward.

The real contrarian risk is in the consensus carry trade: with this cross the best carry-to-volatility trade in the G10, it is a natural candidate for liquidation in any volatility shock, and that unwind would overwhelm the Australian-dollar short covering.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: External positions differ more in this pair than in almost any other G10 cross. Australia ran a record A$27.2bn current-account deficit in the June quarter, 3.67% of GDP. Switzerland ran a CHF 23.7bn surplus, 9.2% of GDP, and holds a net international investment position of CHF 986bn. Direct bilateral trade is small. IMF data show Australian goods exports to Switzerland of USD 1.4bn and imports of USD 3.0bn in 2024, a USD 1.6bn Australian deficit. Swiss-reported flows differ (USD 4.6bn of imports from Australia), most likely because of gold routing. Either way this is not a structural flow driver for the pair. The transmission is through terms of trade. Iron ore, about 35% of Australian export revenue, was near USD 90.60 a tonne on 26 October after a two-year low near USD 89.75, and China's PMI slipped to 49.3. Gold, the franc's commodity link, fell 7% in October, a modest offset in the pair's favour. Inside four weeks the only external print is Australia's 5 November September trade release, which the AUD dossier expects to show a surplus below A$2bn. Both dossiers point the same way, Bearish AUD and Bullish CHF, so the factor is Bearish for the pair at a low tactical weight.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: External balance is the largest strategic negative for the pair. Australia's deficit, the widest since 2016, was built before iron ore hit its two-year low, so the September-quarter balance of payments on 1 December should widen further. Switzerland's surplus generates roughly CHF 70-95bn a year of foreign income that has to be recycled or converted, and the IMF projects a 6.2% of GDP surplus for 2026. Iron ore has structural headwinds from Simandou supply and Chinese property weakness, and the AUD dossier expects USD 82-90 a tonne by the March quarter. With Hormuz disruption persisting, Australia also pays more for fuel imports, while energy is only about 3.5% of the Swiss CPI basket. Real-exchange-rate signals point the same way. The BIS real effective rate is 116.13 for Australia, near the top of its recent range and up 8.77 points in a year, and 98.37 for Switzerland, its lowest in 33 months. So the Australian dollar is real-expensive and the franc real-cheap on recent history. PPP points the other way, putting fair value well above spot, but PPP gaps of this size have no record of closing within six months and are not weighted here. A widening deficit financed by a carry premium that has stopped widening, against a surplus currency whose real rate is cheap, is a classic setup for the pair to fall over one to six months.

net_commodity_exposure.base_commodity_profile: AUD: iron ore (about 35% of export revenue, strongly positive when prices rise), coal and LNG (positive), gold (mildly positive as an exporter); net fuel importer, so an oil supply shock lowers national income even though the framework rule gives oil a mild positive.
net_commodity_exposure.quote_commodity_profile: CHF: no material commodity exports; gold correlates with the franc through the safe-haven channel (gold up is franc-positive); a net energy importer with low energy intensity (about 3.5% of the CPI basket), so oil moves the franc mainly through global risk and inflation.
net_commodity_exposure.net_effect_calculation: Iron ore: up is ++AUD and roughly neutral for CHF, so the net is strongly bullish for the pair; the current two-year low near USD 90.60 is therefore strongly bearish. Gold: up is +CHF and mildly positive for AUD as a producer, so the net is mildly bearish for the pair; October's 7% fall is mildly bullish. Oil: the framework rule gives +AUD (mild) and no direct CHF effect, so the mechanical net is mildly bullish for the pair. But the current episode is a supply shock driven by Hormuz, and the AUD dossier finds the fuel import bill and Asian demand hit outweigh LNG and coal gains, while the same shock raises haven demand for the franc. Net across the three: iron ore dominates and is negative, gold is a small positive offset, and oil is close to neutral or mildly negative in this regime. The overall commodity signal is bearish for AUD/CHF. Bilateral investment context supports the trade-data reading: Swiss sources describe Switzerland's imports from Australia as mainly precious metals, alongside agricultural and pharmaceutical products, consistent with gold routing explaining the gap between the two countries' reported figures.
net_commodity_exposure.scenario_oil_up_10pct: Mechanically mildly bullish for the pair under the framework rule (AUD LNG and coal gains). In the current supply-shock regime it is more likely mildly bearish, because higher fuel import costs, weaker Asian demand and a firmer franc haven bid outweigh energy export gains.
net_commodity_exposure.scenario_oil_down_10pct: If driven by a Hormuz settlement, bullish for the pair: Australia's fuel bill falls, global growth expectations improve and haven demand for the franc fades. If driven by a global demand collapse, bearish, because risk-off dominates.
net_commodity_exposure.dominant_commodity_driver: Iron ore, the largest single channel to Australian national income, with no offsetting franc exposure.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The two banks' communication diverges, and the tactical window contains only one of them. The RBA has turned decisively hawkish. The 29 September statement committed the Board to raising rates further if needed. Deputy Governor Hauser called the inflation outlook materially worse than forecast and warned that businesses were treating 3-3.5% inflation as normal. Board votes have hardened from 5-4 in March to 9-0 in September. The 3 November decision comes with the RBA's quarterly forecasts, according to press reports, so it is the highest-signal event of the four weeks. The year-end trimmed-mean forecast must rise from 3.3% toward 3.7%. The SNB's last word was the 22 October summary of deliberations, which dropped the increased willingness to intervene: mildly franc-positive, but already a week old and partly absorbed. The SNB says nothing scheduled until 10 December, outside the tactical window. With the market pricing only about 0.9 hikes over twelve months, a Board that keeps a live tightening bias would surprise in the pair's favour, while a hike framed as the last would roughly match pricing. The sequencing favours the Australian side, so the factor is Bullish tactically.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months the direction of guidance turns against the pair, even though RBA credibility remains high. The AUD dossier expects the RBA to move to a neutral bias by its 9 February 2027 decision as unemployment rises. That shift is now largely priced, since twelve-month pricing has little beyond November, so it costs the pair less than the dossier assumed. The SNB's guidance is drifting the other way. The 10 December quarterly assessment brings a new conditional forecast. The September version already raised medium-term inflation, partly because of the weaker franc, and the CHF dossier expects December to lift 2027 inflation to 0.9-1.0%, which weakens the case for a zero rate while every peer has tightened. Dropping the increased willingness to intervene also removes a cap on franc strength, though the SNB keeps intervention available as needed. The unpriced guidance surprise over the horizon therefore sits mainly on the Swiss side and is hawkish, while the Australian side is moving from tightening to neutral. That convergence is mildly Bearish for the pair. Confidence is held at 52 because the SNB has a record of reversing its intervention language quickly when the franc strengthens sharply.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: Three events land on 3 November: the RBA decision in the Asian session, Swiss October CPI in the European morning, and the US midterm elections. That clustering will magnify whichever way the day breaks. The geopolitical risks are lopsided for this pair because the main shocks move both legs the same way. A Hormuz escalation that lifts Brent above USD 125 hurts Australian terms of trade and growth while raising haven demand for the franc. October saw the most attacks on shipping in and around the strait since 2017, and the SNB names the Middle East as its main risk. A French government collapse, which the CHF dossier puts at 15% over four weeks, would mainly lift the franc against the euro but would also spill into the pair through broader haven demand. The positive tail is a ceasefire that drops Brent below USD 95, which the AUD dossier also gives about 15%. With the Iran conflict and the European fiscal stress both feeding the franc's haven role, and only one of the tails favouring the pair, the four-week event skew is mildly negative. Australian domestic political risk is low, and Swiss votes on 29 November are not macro events.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over six months the AUD dossier's base case is that the oil shock persists (50%), with settlement and escalation at 25% each. Persistence itself is a slow drain on Australian national income and keeps the franc's haven option alive, so the central case tilts against the pair. US-China trade relations are a second channel specific to the Australian dollar. China's weak PMI leaves Australia's largest export market exposed to any post-midterm tariff escalation, with no equivalent exposure on the Swiss side, where the 15% US tariff arrangement on goods and pharmaceuticals has removed the tariff shock risk. On the franc side, the EU treaty package moving through the Swiss parliament and the bank capital debate are not market-moving within the horizon. The European sovereign stress could fade, which would trim the franc's haven premium, and Chinese policy events (the Central Economic Work Conference in December and the National People's Congress in March) are the main upside catalysts. Both under-delivered for iron ore in 2026. On balance the persistence base case gives a marginal Bearish tilt.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: Fiscal risk is not material for this pair. Australia's 2025-26 deficit was A$22.3bn, 0.8% of GDP, with gross debt at 33.2% of GDP and AAA ratings from all three agencies; S&P reaffirmed in August. Switzerland's general government debt is about 38% of GDP on IMF projections, the federal budget ran a small surplus in 2025, and it is AAA or Aaa stable across agencies. Neither sovereign has a risk premium: the Australian 10-year trades close to Treasuries, and the Swiss 10-year fell 11bp in October on haven demand. The CHF dossier scores fiscal Bullish for the franc, but its argument rests on the contrast with France's widest spread since 2011. That drives allocation from euro assets into francs, not from Australian assets. There is no scheduled fiscal event in either country inside four weeks; Australia's Mid-Year Economic and Fiscal Outlook is due in December. The differential is small and stable, so the factor is Neutral at high confidence.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over six months the fiscal gap between the two sovereigns stays small. Australia's budget projects deficits widening to about A$31bn in 2026-27, and lower iron ore prices threaten mining tax receipts with a lag. The December Mid-Year Economic and Fiscal Outlook is the first official update at sub-USD 95 iron ore and may add A$5-10bn to projected deficits. That would still leave Australia with one of the lowest debt ratios in the G10. Switzerland faces structural federal deficits of CHF 2-4bn a year from 2027 before relief measures, plus defence and pension pressures, but these are below 0.5% of GDP and contained by the debt brake. Both countries have ample fiscal room to cushion a downturn. Mildly expansionary Australian fiscal policy alongside RBA tightening keeps rates higher for longer, a marginal positive through the rate channel already counted in Factor 1. Neither trajectory threatens a rating. The factor stays Neutral; a deficit forecast above 2% of GDP in Australia's December update would be the trigger for a Bearish reading.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: No option is listed on AUD/CHF, so the volatility picture comes from an estimate built from listed CME Australian-dollar and Swiss-franc options and the realised correlation of the two dollar legs. That estimate puts at-the-money implied volatility at 7.293% for about one month, 7.653% for three months and 8.184% for six months, observed 29 October. This is a gentle contango with no visible event spike, and since such estimates have run 9-18% low against direct quotes, true implied volatility is probably nearer 8-9%. The AUD dossier puts the cross's 60-day realised volatility at 7.06%, so the estimated implied barely exceeds realised. The more informative signal is the skew. One-month 25-delta risk reversals are -0.885 vols on AUD/USD (Australian-dollar puts bid) and -0.80 vols on USD/CHF (franc calls bid). Both point the same way for the cross, so the implied skew for AUD/CHF is strongly toward downside protection, larger than on either leg. Protection against a fall in the pair is therefore well owned and relatively expensive, while upside optionality is cheap. That is a statement about how the pair trades, not about its direction, so the factor is Neutral. strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over six months the structure is a low-volatility carry regime with fat tails. The estimated term structure rises from 7.293% to 8.184%, pricing a gradual increase in uncertainty rather than a specific event. The underlying legs show the same: AUD/USD six-month implied volatility is 7.969% and USD/CHF 7.25%. Six-month risk reversals stay negative for the cross on both legs (AUD/USD -1.091 vols, USD/CHF -0.68 vols), so hedgers pay more for pair downside at longer tenors, consistent with the external-balance concern and the Australian-dollar asset-manager short. Franc volatility is known for fat tails, with episodes like the 2015 floor exit, so low implied volatility understates extreme moves in a franc cross. The cross is also less liquid than either dollar leg, which widens gap risk in an unwind. A regime of low realised volatility rewards carry, but the skew shows the market already pays for the reversal. With no directional information in the structure itself, the factor is Neutral.

It is more efficiently expressed through relative value against lower-carry Australian-dollar crosses, or by reducing carry longs, than by an outright short.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: Dollar funding reaches this cross through asymmetry, not directly. Global dollar liquidity is tightening at the margin. Reserve balances fell USD 59.5bn to USD 2,962.6bn in the week to 21 October, below the USD 3tn level many treat as the edge of ample. SOFR printed 3.94%, about 6bp above effective fed funds. The broad dollar is at the 91st percentile of its one-year range, and year-end funding pressure usually builds from late November. A dollar squeeze hits the two legs unequally. Australian banks rely on offshore wholesale funding, and the Australian dollar is the high-beta currency that sells first in a funding scramble. Switzerland holds large net foreign assets (NIIP CHF 986bn), and repatriation in stress tends to support the franc after a brief initial dip. There is no sign of stress in the cross itself: the CME futures roll of about 508.7bp annualised sits about 25-30bp above the expected post-November policy gap, consistent with a small basis and no visible Australian-dollar funding strain. Calm funding keeps franc-funded carry comfortable today, but the direction of travel into year-end is tighter, and that asymmetry tilts the factor mildly against the pair.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over six months the dollar smile frames the factor. Today the dollar sits on its strong side, with US yields near 5%, an oil shock that favours the energy-independent US, and two FOMC dissents for a hike. A 9 December Fed hike, which the dossiers put at 40-55%, would extend that. In that regime the Australian dollar underperforms more than the franc, which is a low-yielder but backed by a large external surplus and net foreign assets. The other path is a dovish post-midterm repricing that takes the dollar toward the middle of the smile. The Australian dollar would gain more there, but the AUD dossier argues it gains less in a soft dollar decline than it loses in a funding squeeze. Fed balance-sheet runoff has ended, so a 2019-style liquidity squeeze is less likely, but reserves below USD 3tn make year-end and March quarter-end pressure plausible. The two banks' differing funding structures, Australian offshore borrowers against Swiss net lenders, keep the asymmetry slightly against the pair. At its reduced weight the factor is mildly Bearish.

tactical.score_interpretation: A net score of +0.084 falls inside the Neutral band, 0.016 short of a Bullish call. Policy and rates (+0.1566), positioning (+0.053) and RBA guidance (+0.0399) are almost matched by risk appetite (-0.077), external balance (-0.033), dollar funding (-0.03) and event risk (-0.0255). Three factors score zero. The bullish tilt comes from one dated event, the 3 November RBA decision, rather than breadth, so the score is fragile to that single outcome. +0.084 lies between -0.10 and +0.10, so the stance is Neutral; conviction 2 reflects measurable, dated forces on both sides rather than an absence of signal.
tactical.rationale: At tactical weights the view is set by policy and rates (0.27), inflation and growth (0.18) and risk appetite (0.14), which together carry 59% of the weight. Policy is Bullish at 58: the 460bp differential is the widest in the G10 and should widen to 485bp on 3 November. But about 80% of that hike is priced, which caps the contribution at +0.1566. Inflation and growth scores zero because hot Australian inflation and a cracking labour market cancel out around the hike. Risk appetite is the main offset at -0.077, because this cross carries double beta: credit spreads at the 95th-96th percentiles of their one-year ranges, a China PMI of 49.3 and an active franc haven bid all push the pair down. The net score of +0.084 is Neutral, the honest reading of a market where the bullish rate news is mostly priced and the bearish risk and terms-of-trade news is not. The two dossiers interact through carry and haven. The AUD dossier's hike and extreme short base reinforce the upside on a hawkish RBA. The CHF dossier's haven bid and leveraged-fund franc short reinforce the downside in a risk-off. The cross-specific modifier is that both legs' options skews point the same way, so protection against a fall is already expensive. What is priced is a hike with little to follow. The edge is a retained tightening bias in the RBA's new forecasts, which twelve-month pricing of only about 0.9 hikes does not reflect. Into 3 November the path of least resistance is sideways with carry accruing. The decision decides the step, and the late-November Australian labour force and 25 November CPI decide whether it holds. Conviction is 2, not 1, because the forces on each side are measurable and dated. It is not 3 because the score rests on one event and the risk backdrop is deteriorating at the same time.
tactical.g10_relative_ranking: Among Australian-dollar crosses, AUD/CHF ranks as the most attractive tactical long on a carry-adjusted basis (ratio near 0.60). It sits ahead of AUD/JPY, which faces a live 18 December BoJ hike, and far ahead of AUD/NOK and AUD/CAD, where oil favours the quote currency. Among franc-funded carry, it ranks behind NOK/CHF, which combines a 450bp gap with oil terms of trade, and roughly level with GBP/CHF. strategic.score_interpretation: A net score of -0.1411 is Bearish, clearing the threshold by 0.041. The result comes from breadth, not depth: five factors with confidence of 51-64 (external balance -0.1024, guidance -0.0624, inflation and growth -0.055, dollar funding -0.0357, event risk -0.026) outweigh a single strong positive, carry (+0.1404). The score speaks to direction only. The pair's roughly 5% annualised forward discount means a short must beat the carry, so a modest bearish drift could still lose money for a short holder. -0.1411 is at or below -0.10, so the stance is Bearish; conviction is 2 because the score clears the threshold by only 0.041 and the highest-weight factor points the other way.
strategic.rationale: At strategic weights policy and rates still carries the most weight at 0.27 and is the single largest contribution at +0.1404, because a 485bp differential after November remains the best carry in the G10. But external balance rises to 0.16 and guidance to 0.12, and both turn against the pair. External balance contributes -0.1024: a record 3.67% of GDP Australian current-account deficit and iron ore near a two-year low, against a 9.2% of GDP Swiss surplus and a Swiss real exchange rate at its lowest in 33 months. Guidance contributes -0.0624, because the next unpriced policy surprise is a hawkish SNB forecast on 10 December, while the RBA is heading toward a neutral bias the market already prices. The net -0.1411 is Bearish at conviction 2, driven by breadth across slow-moving structural factors rather than one dominant input. The dossiers conflict on the base side and reinforce on the quote side. The AUD dossier is strategically Neutral only because carry and positioning offset its bearish external and growth view. The CHF dossier is Bullish on the franc for exactly the reasons that weigh on this pair: surplus, guidance drift and rising inflation. The cross-specific modifiers are that fiscal strength barely matters here, since the franc's fiscal bid is against the euro, and that risk appetite transmits with double beta, which sharpens tails without setting direction. What is priced is an RBA peak at 4.85% and an SNB on hold into mid-2027. Our edge is that Swiss inflation and the 10 December forecast round open a 2027 hike option the curve does not price, while Australian terms of trade keep deteriorating. The path of least resistance is carry-supported stability through year-end, then erosion from the 1 December Australian balance of payments, the 2 December GDP and the 10 December SNB assessment, with the RBA's 9 February decision as the last scheduled inflection inside the window. Conviction is held at 2 because the highest-weight factor points the other way, the forward discount makes a bearish view costly to hold, and the extreme Australian-dollar short limits how fast the pair can fall.
strategic.g10_relative_ranking: Strategically, AUD/CHF ranks among the weaker Australian-dollar longs. The AUD dossier ranks the Australian dollar seventh of eleven and the CHF dossier ranks the franc fourth, so the combination points to the pair falling. Better bearish expressions of the Australian terms-of-trade theme are AUD/NOK (10bp carry cost, oil favours NOK) and AUD/NZD, both far cheaper to hold than an AUD/CHF short, which carries a 485bp cost. Among franc crosses, the CHF dossier prefers short GBP/CHF and short CHF/JPY to short AUD/CHF, because the latter's carry makes timing essential.

consensus_divergence.our_tactical_view: Neutral, with a slight upward tilt resting on the 3 November RBA decision and its new forecasts. Carry accrues while the hiking story holds, and deteriorating credit and a franc haven bid limit the upside.
consensus_divergence.our_strategic_view: Bearish at conviction 2: external-balance, growth and guidance convergence outweigh the carry advantage over one to six months, with the pair expected to drift lower once Australian rate momentum fades.
consensus_divergence.divergence_direction: Not measurable against a pair consensus. Against the leg forecasts in the dossiers, we are less constructive on the Australian dollar than Westpac and ING (AUD/USD 0.72), closer to CBA's bearish path, and more constructive on the franc than UBS (EUR/CHF 0.95 by end-2026).
consensus_divergence.divergence_magnitude: Not measurable: no bank research forecast for AUD/CHF was located, and combining different banks' forecasts for the two dollar legs does not make a pair consensus.
consensus_divergence.why_we_differ: We found no bank forecast for this cross. The pages that publish AUD/CHF projections are statistical extrapolation sites, not bank research, and are not used. Against the leg views, we differ in two ways. First, the bullish Australian-dollar forecasts near 0.72 against the dollar assume a terms-of-trade recovery that iron ore futures near a two-year low do not support. Second, bank franc-weakening forecasts set before October treat the franc purely as a funding currency and ignore the SNB's retreat from intervention and the 2027 hike option that rising Swiss inflation creates. Those two disagreements both point to AUD/CHF falling relative to what the leg consensus implies. Additional context: ExchangeRates.org.uk, which says its CHF/AUD projections blend aggregated bank research, market expectations and a sentiment survey, projects CHF/AUD at 1.7393 by December 2026 and 1.7549 by March 2027, i.e. about 0.5749 and 0.5698 for AUD/CHF (49 and 100 pips below spot, same direction as our strategic view). Because it blends sentiment and its baseline appears to predate October, it does not establish a bank consensus and is noted as context only. Purely statistical sites such as Traders Union (AUD/CHF near 0.5729 by end-2026) are model extrapolations and are not used.
consensus_divergence.payoff_if_right: If the structural factors dominate, the pair drifts lower through early 2027. The cleanest benefit is to holders who cut carry longs early or express Australian-dollar weakness through lower-carry crosses, since an outright short pays about 2.3-2.5% in carry over six months.
consensus_divergence.risk_if_wrong: If carry and a hawkish RBA dominate, an outright short loses the spot move plus carry of roughly 0.4% a month, and the extreme Australian-dollar short base makes an upside squeeze sharper than a decline.

cross_horizon_consistency.explanation: The horizons diverge because the weights move from event-driven to structural factors. Tactically, policy, positioning and RBA guidance around 3 November nearly offset risk appetite and external balance. Strategically, external balance rises from 0.06 to 0.16 and guidance from 0.07 to 0.12 and flips to Bearish as SNB guidance drifts hawkish, while positioning falls to Neutral. Carry stays positive throughout but cannot outweigh the breadth of slower negatives over one to six months.
cross_horizon_consistency.inflection_point: The 1-2 December Australian balance of payments and GDP releases, followed by the 10 December SNB quarterly assessment with its new conditional forecast. The RBA's 9 February 2027 decision is the last scheduled confirmation point inside the window.
cross_horizon_consistency.trading_implication: Do not fight the carry before the structural catalysts arrive. Treat any strength after a hawkish 3 November as the window to reduce carry longs, not to add, and let the December data and SNB forecast confirm the strategic bearish turn before expressing it outright. Levels: strength to sell into is the seven-touch band at 0.58123-0.58585; confirmation of the strategic turn is a daily close below the four-touch band at 0.57056; the strategic objective is the six-touch 0.56309-0.5672 band, where the falling 200-week average arrives by February-March 2027. Reservation on payoff, not direction: the six-month forward of 0.56508 already sits inside that band, so a bearish outcome that stops there pays an outright short almost nothing after carry; the call is publishable as a direction and a reason to cut carry exposure, not as a strong case for an outright short. Realised volatility (20-day 8.74%) above the one-month implied estimate (7.293%), plus the chart's run of large down-days, suggests the tactical risk-appetite drag may be understated.

catalysts.rationale: A 25bp hike to 4.85% is priced at about 79-81%. The pair's edge is in guidance: with only about 0.9 hikes priced over twelve months, a retained tightening bias and upgraded trimmed-mean forecasts would widen the expected differential and trigger covering of the extreme Australian-dollar short. A hold, about one chance in five, would take roughly 20bp off the front end.

September CPI was 1.0% and core 0.5%. A print of 1.2% or higher would revive SNB hike pricing for 10 December from about 6bp and weigh on the pair. A print of 0.8% or lower would cement the zero rate as a funding anchor and support carry. It lands hours after the RBA decision.

The result moves the cross through risk appetite and the dollar smile rather than directly. A dovish Fed repricing and a softer dollar would favour the higher-beta Australian dollar, while a risk-off reaction or tariff escalation toward China would lift the franc and hurt Australian demand.

assumptions: Price series: daily closing prices for AUD/CHF, 130 weekday sessions from 2026-05-04 to 2026-10-30; spot is 0.57979 at the 30 October 2026 close. The 1 November valuation date is a Sunday, so no trading session lies between the last close and the valuation date. Moving averages and support/resistance zones are computed over the full weekday history: 4,920 daily sessions from 2007-12-24 to 2026-10-30, with 1,011 weekly and 502 monthly bars.

Moving averages are simple averages of trading-day closes; realised volatility is annualised on 252 trading days; ATR(14) is 47 pips. Zones are clusters of weekly and monthly swing closes, ranked by touch count, with distances to the zone centre. The 52-week percentile is quoted on a closing basis (91st); intraday basis is 89th.
The time spent above the 200-week average and the dates on which it meets the support bands are back-projected at its current slope of -2.94 pips a week and are approximations.

Rates: the 10-year yields of 5.283% (Australia) and 0.59% (Switzerland) are monthly readings as of 1 September and are not quoted as live levels. Live spreads use 30 October daily closes (Australia 4.93% 2-year and 5.137% 10-year; Switzerland 0.18% and 0.47%). Policy rates are the RBA's 4.60% (29 September) and the SNB's 0% (24 September).

RBA pricing uses the latest readings: about 79-81% for a 3 November hike and about 0.9 hikes net over twelve months, as of 1 November, superseding the 85-88% in the AUD dossier measured straight after the 28 October CPI. The RBA's 3 November quarterly forecasts are taken from press reports. A possible SNB move in March 2027 falls beyond the schedule covered and is not tied to a date.

No option is listed on the cross. Implied volatility of 7.293% (35.7 days), 7.653% (98.7 days) and 8.184% (189.6 days) is an estimate from listed options on the two dollar legs and a 0.39 realised correlation, observed 29 October. Such estimates have run 9-18% low, so it is treated as a floor. No implied-volatility percentile is available for the cross.

The 508.7bp futures calendar roll (Dec 2026 to Mar 2027 contracts, observed 29 October) combines the rate differential and any cross-currency basis, which cannot be separated without an OIS curve. In the structured fields it is entered as annualised carry earned by a long (+508.7bp, the AUD at a forward discount), with carry-to-vol 0.66 on that basis; the 0.60 ratio on the 460bp policy differential is the alternative. Forward points use an actual/365 basis for 30, 91 and 182 days.

Weights: Factor 1 +0.03 (high carry), Factor 3 +0.04 (risk-proxy cross), Factor 8 -0.02 (no fiscal differential between two AAA sovereigns), Factor 10 -0.05 (non-USD cross). Both horizons sum to 1.00.

The framework's oil rule gives the Australian dollar a mild positive. Because the current oil shock is a supply disruption that the AUD dossier finds harmful to Australian terms of trade, oil is treated as near neutral to mildly negative for the pair in this regime.

Bilateral trade uses IMF Direction of Trade 2024 goods data. The mismatch between Australian-reported exports to Switzerland and Swiss-reported imports from Australia is attributed to gold routing and not reconciled.

PPP fair value (about 0.6653) and BIS real effective rates point in opposite directions. Neither is weighted directly; the REER evidence supports the Factor 5 strategic stance only as secondary evidence.
